title: Coordinate Span Calculator: Spread of Points
description: Measure the span of a set of coordinates with the Coordinate Span Calculator — north-south and east-west extents in degrees and distance. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square to JFK spans 21.77 km corner-to-corner — but its latitude span (0.117°) and longitude span (0.207°) tell the shape of the spread, not just its size.
quick_answer: The Coordinate Span Calculator measures how far a set of coordinates spreads — the north-south and east-west extents in degrees and in ground distance, with the diagonal for scale. Paste the points and read the span — the footprint's dimensions, deciding zooms, boxes and sampling density.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The extents of a coordinate set: latitude and longitude spans in degrees, their ground distances, and the corner-to-corner diagonal.
Which map standard does it use?
WGS84 coordinates with spherical distances — the web-mapping standard this family shares.
Can I use this in production GIS?
As footprint characterisation, yes — it matches GIS extent statistics. Production pipelines compute it natively; this page is the independent check.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
Span inherits the points' accuracy; one wild point dominates it entirely — which the outlier use case turns into a feature.
Date-line sets?
A set straddling ±180° needs longitude unwrapping; the calculator's handling follows the smallest-covering-arc logic rather than naively spanning 358°.
Span or bounding box?
The box is the span's rectangle (min/max) — same extremes, different packaging. This page reports dimensions; the generator packages queries.
Two points only?
Perfectly valid — the span of a pair is their separation decomposed into axes plus the diagonal distance.
Weighted centre versus span centre?
The box centre is the extremes' middle; the mean is the points' centre. They differ whenever the set is lopsided — report the one your claim uses.
Units?
Degrees always; ground distance in km and miles, per convention.
Empty middle problem?
Span cannot see holes. Density questions need the points themselves — span is the footprint's ruler, not its portrait.
